lessons.title: Author purpose and audience
lessons.objective: Identify why a text was written and who it is for.

introduce.text: Authors write for a reason: to inform, to persuade or to entertain. Knowing the purpose helps you read with the right mind.
introduce.speech: Authors write for a reason: to inform, to persuade or to entertain. Knowing the purpose helps you read with the right mind.

introduce.text: The audience is the reader the text is meant for. Word choice and tone give clues: simple words for young children, formal words for officers.
introduce.speech: The audience is the reader the text is meant for. Word choice and tone give clues: simple words for young children, formal words for officers.

demonstrate.text: Read: 'Buy a Lakshmi cycle today! It is the strongest cycle in town, so you must not miss this offer.' The pushing words show the purpose is to persuade.
demonstrate.speech: Read: 'Buy a Lakshmi cycle today! It is the strongest cycle in town, so you must not miss this offer.' The pushing words show the purpose is to persuade.

demonstrate.text: Read: 'The Ganga is about 2,500 km long and flows through five states.' It gives plain facts and pushes nothing, so the purpose is to inform.
demonstrate.speech: Read: 'The Ganga is about 2,500 km long and flows through five states.' It gives plain facts and pushes nothing, so the purpose is to inform.

guided.prompt: A poster says: 'Polio drops for children under five. Sunday, 8 am to 4 pm, at the Anganwadi.' What is its purpose?
guided.speech: A poster says: 'Polio drops for children under five. Sunday, 8 am to 4 pm, at the Anganwadi.' What is its purpose?
options: To tell parents about an event
guided.answer: To tell parents about an event
hints: Does it push an opinion, or just state time and place?
Time, date and place are facts given to help readers.

wrong_feedback.To make readers laugh: There is no joke; the poster only gives plain details.
wrong_feedback.To argue against vaccines: Nothing in the poster argues against anything.

guided.explanation: The poster gives time and place so parents know when to come.

guided.prompt: A magazine for ten-year-olds begins: 'Guess what! A tiny frog just hopped onto my homework!' Who is the likely audience?
guided.speech: A magazine for ten-year-olds begins: 'Guess what! A tiny frog just hopped onto my homework!' Who is the likely audience?
guided.answer: Children who like funny stories
hints: Look at the tone: is it chatty and playful or formal?
Playful words and a funny event suit young readers.

wrong_feedback.Retired bank officers: A playful tone like this does not suit formal readers.
wrong_feedback.Doctors reading a journal: A medical journal would not say 'Guess what!'.

guided.explanation: The chatty, playful tone suits young readers.

practice.prompt: 'Every citizen must vote. It is the only way to build a strong nation!' What is the author's purpose?
practice.speech: 'Every citizen must vote. It is the only way to build a strong nation!' What is the author's purpose?
hints: Which words push the reader to act?
Strong pushing words show the author wants to convince.

wrong_feedback.To tell a bedtime story: This is not a story at all.

practice.explanation: 'Must' and 'the only way' push the reader to act.

practice.prompt: Which is written mainly to entertain?
practice.speech: Which is written mainly to entertain?
options: A comic tale of a clumsy magician
practice.answer: A comic tale of a clumsy magician
hints: Entertain means to amuse. Which would you read for fun?
A story about a clumsy magician is made to be enjoyed.

wrong_feedback.A notice about water cuts: A notice informs; it is not meant for fun.

practice.explanation: A funny tale is meant to be enjoyed.

practice.prompt: A letter begins: 'Respected Principal Madam, I request your kind permission...' Who is it written to?
practice.speech: A letter begins: 'Respected Principal Madam, I request your kind permission...' Who is it written to?
hints: The greeting names a job. What is the job?
'Respected' and 'kind permission' are formal words for someone in charge.

wrong_feedback.A close friend: A friend would get casual words, not 'Respected'.
wrong_feedback.A baby cousin: A baby cannot read this and the tone is far too formal.

practice.explanation: 'Principal' and the polite words show a head of school.

check.prompt: 'Our village well is dry. The panchayat meets on Monday at 5 pm to decide on a new borewell.' What is the purpose?
check.speech: 'Our village well is dry. The panchayat meets on Monday at 5 pm to decide on a new borewell.' What is the purpose?
options: To inform villagers of a meeting
check.answer: To inform villagers of a meeting

wrong_feedback.To entertain with a riddle: There is no riddle or joke.

check.explanation: It gives the day, time and reason for a meeting.

check.prompt: 'Switch off the fan when you leave. It is the smartest habit, and every student should follow it!' The author wants to...
check.speech: 'Switch off the fan when you leave. It is the smartest habit, and every student should follow it!' The author wants to...

wrong_feedback.tell a ghost story: There is no story or ghost.

check.prompt: Which clue shows a text is for very young children?
check.speech: Which clue shows a text is for very young children?

wrong_feedback.Long legal terms: Legal terms suit adults, not young children.

check.explanation: Young readers need easy words and short lines.

explain.text: Think of a text as a letter. Someone sends it for a reason (the purpose) to someone (the audience). Your job is to guess both.
explain.speech: Think of a text as a letter. Someone sends it for a reason (the purpose) to someone (the audience). Your job is to guess both.

explain.text: Read: 'Come to our Diwali mela! Best sweets, best games, the best day of your year. Do not miss it!' Words like 'best' and 'Do not miss' show it persuades.
explain.speech: Read: 'Come to our Diwali mela! Best sweets, best games, the best day of your year. Do not miss it!' Words like 'best' and 'Do not miss' show it persuades.

explain.text: Ask two questions: Why was this written? Who is it written for? Tone and word choice give the clues.
explain.speech: Ask two questions: Why was this written? Who is it written for? Tone and word choice give the clues.

guided.prompt: A bus stand board says: 'Bus to Hyderabad leaves at 6 pm from platform 3.' Its purpose is...
guided.speech: A bus stand board says: 'Bus to Hyderabad leaves at 6 pm from platform 3.' Its purpose is...
guided.answer: to give information
hints: Does it push an opinion or just give facts?
A time and a platform are plain facts for travellers.

wrong_feedback.to sell tickets by force: It does not pressure anyone to buy.
wrong_feedback.to make people laugh: There is nothing funny in it.

guided.explanation: It states a time and place without pushing anything.

guided.prompt: A comic strip shows a goat stealing a hat. The audience is probably...
guided.speech: A comic strip shows a goat stealing a hat. The audience is probably...
guided.answer: children who like fun
hints: Is the content serious or silly?
Silly stories are written for readers who enjoy fun.

wrong_feedback.tax officers: A silly strip is not made for formal readers.
wrong_feedback.engineers checking a bridge: Nothing here relates to bridge work.

guided.explanation: A silly picture story is made for readers who like to laugh.

check.prompt: 'Plant a tree today! Trees are the best gift for our children!' The purpose is to...
check.speech: 'Plant a tree today! Trees are the best gift for our children!' The purpose is to...
check.explanation: 'Plant' and 'best' push the reader to act.

check.prompt: A science book says: 'Sound travels as waves through air.' The author wants to...
check.speech: A science book says: 'Sound travels as waves through air.' The author wants to...
check.explanation: It states a fact and nothing more.

check.prompt: A letter says: 'Dear Grandma, I miss you. Come soon!' Who is the audience?
check.speech: A letter says: 'Dear Grandma, I miss you. Come soon!' Who is the audience?

wrong_feedback.a shopkeeper: A shopkeeper is not named or addressed.
wrong_feedback.a police officer: The letter is personal, not an official one.

check.explanation: The letter begins by naming her.

lessons.title: Fact, opinion and evidence
lessons.objective: Tell facts from opinions and find evidence for a claim.

introduce.text: A fact can be checked and proved true or false, like 'Delhi is the capital of India.' An opinion is what someone believes or feels, like 'Delhi is the nicest city.'
introduce.speech: A fact can be checked and proved true or false, like 'Delhi is the capital of India.' An opinion is what someone believes or feels, like 'Delhi is the nicest city.'

introduce.text: Evidence is proof that supports a claim: a number, a record or an example. Strong claims have strong evidence.
introduce.speech: Evidence is proof that supports a claim: a number, a record or an example. Strong claims have strong evidence.

demonstrate.text: Read: 'The Taj Mahal was finished around 1653. It is the most beautiful building in India.' The first sentence can be checked in books, so it is a fact. 'Most beautiful' is a feeling, so it is an opinion.
demonstrate.speech: Read: 'The Taj Mahal was finished around 1653. It is the most beautiful building in India.' The first sentence can be checked in books, so it is a fact. 'Most beautiful' is a feeling, so it is an opinion.

demonstrate.text: Claim: 'Our bus is often late.' Weak support: 'I hate waiting.' Strong evidence: 'It was late on 9 of the last 10 days.' Numbers that can be checked make evidence strong.
demonstrate.speech: Claim: 'Our bus is often late.' Weak support: 'I hate waiting.' Strong evidence: 'It was late on 9 of the last 10 days.' Numbers that can be checked make evidence strong.

guided.prompt: Which sentence is a FACT?
guided.speech: Which sentence is a FACT?
guided.answer: A week has seven days
hints: Can you check it in a calendar or book, or is it a feeling?
Only one sentence can be proved true by counting.

wrong_feedback.Mondays are the worst days: 'Worst' is a feeling, so it is an opinion.
wrong_feedback.Seven is a lucky number: Luck is a belief; nobody can prove it.

guided.explanation: You can check this on any calendar.

guided.prompt: Which sentence is an OPINION?
guided.speech: Which sentence is an OPINION?
options: Idli is made from rice and urad dal
guided.answer: Idli is the tastiest breakfast
hints: Look for a word that judges, not one that measures.
People can disagree about taste, so one sentence is an opinion.

wrong_feedback.Idli is made from rice and urad dal: Ingredients can be checked, so this is a fact.

guided.explanation: 'Tastiest' depends on who is eating.

practice.prompt: Claim: 'Cycling to school is good for health.' Which is the best evidence?
practice.speech: Claim: 'Cycling to school is good for health.' Which is the best evidence?
options: A doctor's study found cyclists had stronger hearts
practice.answer: A doctor's study found cyclists had stronger hearts
hints: Evidence must be checkable and linked to health.
A study by a doctor measures real results.

wrong_feedback.My neighbour loves cycling: One person's liking is not proof.

practice.explanation: A study measures real results.

practice.prompt: Which word often signals an opinion?
practice.speech: Which word often signals an opinion?
hints: Opinion words judge things as good or bad.
Facts use measures and dates; one option judges.

wrong_feedback.kilogram: A kilogram is a measure, which belongs to facts.
wrong_feedback.yesterday: 'Yesterday' names a time, which belongs to facts.

practice.explanation: 'Greatest' judges something, so people may disagree.

practice.prompt: Seema says, 'Our school needs a bigger playground.' Which would make her claim stronger?
practice.speech: Seema says, 'Our school needs a bigger playground.' Which would make her claim stronger?
options: Saying it is a big problem
Counting that 400 students share one small ground
practice.answer: Counting that 400 students share one small ground
hints: Strong evidence is something you can count or show.
A count of how many students share the space supports the claim.

wrong_feedback.Saying it is a big problem: Repeating a claim is not evidence.
wrong_feedback.Asking friends to nod: Agreement from friends is not proof.

practice.explanation: A count is real evidence.

check.prompt: Which is a FACT?
check.speech: Which is a FACT?
check.explanation: A height can be measured and checked.

check.prompt: 'The new park is popular.' Which evidence best supports this claim?
check.speech: 'The new park is popular.' Which evidence best supports this claim?
options: The park has a nice gate
The park was built by the municipality

wrong_feedback.The park has a nice gate: A gate does not show popularity.
wrong_feedback.The park was built by the municipality: It is true but does not show popularity.

check.explanation: A count shows how popular it is.

check.prompt: Which sentence mixes a fact with an opinion?
check.speech: Which sentence mixes a fact with an opinion?
options: Chennai is on the coast and has the loveliest beach
check.answer: Chennai is on the coast and has the loveliest beach

wrong_feedback.Chennai is on the coast: This is only a fact in 'Chennai is on the coast'.
wrong_feedback.Chennai has a beach: This is only a fact in 'Chennai has a beach'.

check.explanation: 'On the coast' is a fact; 'loveliest' is an opinion.

explain.text: A fact is like a stone: solid, and you can test it. An opinion is like a cloud: it changes with who is looking.
explain.speech: A fact is like a stone: solid, and you can test it. An opinion is like a cloud: it changes with who is looking.

explain.text: Read: 'Sachin scored 100 centuries. He was the greatest batter.' The count can be checked, so it is a fact. 'Greatest' is an opinion.
explain.speech: Read: 'Sachin scored 100 centuries. He was the greatest batter.' The count can be checked, so it is a fact. 'Greatest' is an opinion.

explain.text: Ask: can I prove this with a number, date or record? If yes, it is a fact. If it depends on feelings, it is an opinion.
explain.speech: Ask: can I prove this with a number, date or record? If yes, it is a fact. If it depends on feelings, it is an opinion.

guided.prompt: Which is a fact?
guided.speech: Which is a fact?
options: The Ganga is the holiest river
The Ganga flows into the Bay of Bengal
guided.answer: The Ganga flows into the Bay of Bengal
hints: Choose the sentence a map could prove.
Where a river ends can be checked on a map.

wrong_feedback.The Ganga is the holiest river: 'Holiest' is a belief, not a measure.

guided.explanation: A map can prove where the river ends.

guided.prompt: Claim: 'Our class reads a lot.' Which is evidence?
guided.speech: Claim: 'Our class reads a lot.' Which is evidence?
options: Each student read 5 books this term
guided.answer: Each student read 5 books this term
hints: Evidence should be a number or record.
A count of books read supports the claim.

wrong_feedback.Reading is fun: This is an opinion about reading.
wrong_feedback.Our class is clever: Cleverness is not proof of reading.

guided.explanation: A count of books is checkable proof.

check.prompt: Which is an opinion?
check.speech: Which is an opinion?
options: Football is more fun than chess
check.answer: Football is more fun than chess

wrong_feedback.A football team has 11 players: A team's size can be checked.

check.prompt: 'Sunita is the fastest runner in Class 7.' Which proves it?
check.speech: 'Sunita is the fastest runner in Class 7.' Which proves it?
options: She won the 100 m race in 13 seconds
check.answer: She won the 100 m race in 13 seconds
check.explanation: A race time is recorded evidence.

check.prompt: Which belongs to a fact rather than an opinion?
check.speech: Which belongs to a fact rather than an opinion?

lessons.title: Inference across paragraphs
lessons.objective: Combine clues from two paragraphs to make an inference.

introduce.text: An inference is a smart guess based on clues in the text. The writer does not say it directly; you work it out.
introduce.speech: An inference is a smart guess based on clues in the text. The writer does not say it directly; you work it out.

introduce.text: Clues may sit in different paragraphs. Collect them, join them, then say what they point to. Always be ready to name the clues.
introduce.speech: Clues may sit in different paragraphs. Collect them, join them, then say what they point to. Always be ready to name the clues.

demonstrate.text: Para 1: Meera's hair was wet and her bag was soaked. Para 2: She hung a dripping raincoat by the door. Clues: wet hair, soaked bag, dripping raincoat. Inference: it was raining outside.
demonstrate.speech: Para 1: Meera's hair was wet and her bag was soaked. Para 2: She hung a dripping raincoat by the door. Clues: wet hair, soaked bag, dripping raincoat. Inference: it was raining outside.

demonstrate.text: A good inference has proof. 'Meera was caught in the rain' has three clues. 'Meera was angry' has no clue, so it is only a wild guess.
demonstrate.speech: A good inference has proof. 'Meera was caught in the rain' has three clues. 'Meera was angry' has no clue, so it is only a wild guess.

guided.prompt: Para 1: Dev kept checking his watch. Para 2: He ran to the gate as the school bell rang. What can we infer?
guided.speech: Para 1: Dev kept checking his watch. Para 2: He ran to the gate as the school bell rang. What can we infer?
options: Dev was worried about being late
Dev wanted to go to sleep
guided.answer: Dev was worried about being late
hints: Join the two clues: what do they suggest together?
Checking time and rushing as the bell rings points to fear of being late.
guided.explanation: Watch-checking and running at the bell point to lateness.

guided.prompt: Para 1: Gita's grandmother stirred a big pot. Para 2: Neighbours kept arriving with plates. What is likely happening?
guided.speech: Para 1: Gita's grandmother stirred a big pot. Para 2: Neighbours kept arriving with plates. What is likely happening?
guided.answer: A feast is being prepared
hints: Think about why many people would bring plates.
A big pot and plates both point to food for a gathering.

wrong_feedback.A power cut is happening: Nothing hints at a power cut.

guided.explanation: A big pot and arriving guests suggest a feast.

practice.prompt: Para 1: Imran's name was called for the prize. Para 2: He walked up with a big smile and shaking hands. How does he feel?
practice.speech: Para 1: Imran's name was called for the prize. Para 2: He walked up with a big smile and shaking hands. How does he feel?
hints: Look at both his face and his hands.
A smile and shaking hands together show mixed feelings.

wrong_feedback.Bored and sleepy: A big smile does not show boredom.
wrong_feedback.Angry and upset: A smile does not show anger.

practice.explanation: A smile shows pride and shaking hands show nerves.

practice.prompt: Para 1: The dog's bowl was empty. Para 2: It sat by the door wagging its tail as Mohan came home with a packet. What can we infer?
practice.speech: Para 1: The dog's bowl was empty. Para 2: It sat by the door wagging its tail as Mohan came home with a packet. What can we infer?
options: The dog was hungry and expected food
practice.answer: The dog was hungry and expected food
hints: What do an empty bowl and a wagging tail suggest together?
The dog hopes the packet holds food.

wrong_feedback.The dog was sick: A wagging tail does not suggest illness.

practice.explanation: An empty bowl and a wagging tail point to hunger.

practice.prompt: Anu's lamp was on at midnight and books lay open. Which inference has NO clue in the text?
practice.speech: Anu's lamp was on at midnight and books lay open. Which inference has NO clue in the text?
hints: A weak inference has nothing in the text to back it.
Two options match the lamp and books; one matches nothing.

wrong_feedback.Anu is studying late: Open books and a lamp support this.

practice.explanation: Nothing in the text mentions travel.

check.prompt: Para 1: The village road was washed away. Para 2: Boats carried people along the main street. What can we infer?
check.speech: Para 1: The village road was washed away. Para 2: Boats carried people along the main street. What can we infer?
check.explanation: A washed-away road and boats on the street point to flooding.

check.prompt: Para 1: Pooja's room was spotless and her bag was packed. Para 2: She set two alarms. What does this suggest?
check.speech: Para 1: Pooja's room was spotless and her bag was packed. Para 2: She set two alarms. What does this suggest?
options: She has an early morning plan
check.answer: She has an early morning plan

wrong_feedback.She forgot to sleep: Nothing says she forgot to sleep.
wrong_feedback.She dislikes alarms: She set two, so she uses them.

check.explanation: Packing and two alarms suggest early preparation.

check.prompt: What should you do first to back up an inference?
check.speech: What should you do first to back up an inference?

wrong_feedback.Guess from the title alone: A title alone is not enough proof.

check.explanation: An inference must be supported by clues.

explain.text: Be a detective: a detective collects clues before naming who did it. In reading, clues are details and the inference is your conclusion.
explain.speech: Be a detective: a detective collects clues before naming who did it. In reading, clues are details and the inference is your conclusion.

explain.text: Read: Para 1: Farid wore his best kurta. Para 2: He carried sweets to every neighbour. Inference: it is Eid, a festival day.
explain.speech: Read: Para 1: Farid wore his best kurta. Para 2: He carried sweets to every neighbour. Inference: it is Eid, a festival day.

explain.text: Steps: collect clues from every paragraph, join them, state the inference, then name the clue that proves it.
explain.speech: Steps: collect clues from every paragraph, join them, state the inference, then name the clue that proves it.

guided.prompt: Para 1: Lata's school bag was heavy with books. Para 2: She waited at the bus stop in her uniform. What can we infer?
guided.speech: Para 1: Lata's school bag was heavy with books. Para 2: She waited at the bus stop in her uniform. What can we infer?
options: She is going to a wedding
guided.answer: It is a school day
hints: What do a uniform and a bag of books go with?
Both belong to a school day.

wrong_feedback.It is a holiday: A holiday would not need books and a uniform.
wrong_feedback.She is going to a wedding: A uniform does not fit a wedding.

guided.explanation: Books and a uniform suggest school.

guided.prompt: Para 1: A cow stood on the railway track. Para 2: The train driver pressed the horn and slowed down. Why?
guided.speech: Para 1: A cow stood on the railway track. Para 2: The train driver pressed the horn and slowed down. Why?
guided.answer: To avoid hitting the cow
hints: Connect the cow with the driver's actions.
Slowing and hooting are ways of avoiding a collision.

wrong_feedback.To buy tickets: A driver does not buy tickets on the track.
wrong_feedback.To water the engine: Nothing here says anything about water.

guided.explanation: The horn and slowing show he wants to stop in time.

check.prompt: Para 1: Ramu's coat was thick and his breath made clouds. Para 2: He rubbed his hands near a fire. What time of year is it?
check.speech: Para 1: Ramu's coat was thick and his breath made clouds. Para 2: He rubbed his hands near a fire. What time of year is it?

wrong_feedback.Summer: It is far too cold for summer.

check.explanation: Thick coats and misty breath point to cold.

check.prompt: Para 1: Nisha's cheeks were wet. Para 2: She held a torn photo of her pet parrot. How does she feel?
check.speech: Para 1: Nisha's cheeks were wet. Para 2: She held a torn photo of her pet parrot. How does she feel?
check.explanation: Wet cheeks and the torn photo show sadness.

check.prompt: The shutter was down and a board read 'Closed for Diwali'. Which inference is best supported?
check.speech: The shutter was down and a board read 'Closed for Diwali'. Which inference is best supported?
options: The shop is shut for the festival
check.answer: The shop is shut for the festival

introduce.text: Figurative language uses words in a special way, not with their plain meaning. A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'. A metaphor says one thing IS another.
introduce.speech: Figurative language uses words in a special way, not with their plain meaning. A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'. A metaphor says one thing IS another.

introduce.text: Idioms are fixed phrases whose meaning is not in the single words, like 'under the weather' meaning unwell. Use the situation to decode them.
introduce.speech: Idioms are fixed phrases whose meaning is not in the single words, like 'under the weather' meaning unwell. Use the situation to decode them.

demonstrate.text: Simile: 'Her voice was as sweet as honey.' It compares using 'as' and tells us the voice was pleasant. Metaphor: 'The classroom was a beehive.' It says one thing IS another: busy and buzzing.
demonstrate.speech: Simile: 'Her voice was as sweet as honey.' It compares using 'as' and tells us the voice was pleasant. Metaphor: 'The classroom was a beehive.' It says one thing IS another: busy and buzzing.

demonstrate.text: Idiom: 'He spilled the beans.' No beans fall; it means he gave away a secret. If the plain meaning sounds silly, look for an idiom.
demonstrate.speech: Idiom: 'He spilled the beans.' No beans fall; it means he gave away a secret. If the plain meaning sounds silly, look for an idiom.

guided.prompt: 'The old man was as slow as a snail.' This is a simile because it...
guided.speech: 'The old man was as slow as a snail.' This is a simile because it...
guided.answer: compares using the word 'as'
hints: Look for the small comparison word in the sentence.
The comparison word links the man and the snail.

wrong_feedback.gives a command: It does not tell anyone to do anything.

guided.explanation: 'As slow as' compares the man to a snail.

guided.prompt: 'She is under the weather today.' What does the idiom mean?
guided.speech: 'She is under the weather today.' What does the idiom mean?
options: She is standing in the rain
guided.answer: She is unwell
hints: If the plain words sound odd, it is an idiom. What would make someone stay home?
The idiom means feeling ill.

wrong_feedback.She is standing in the rain: The phrase is not about rain.
wrong_feedback.She is studying geography: The phrase is not about lessons.

guided.explanation: The phrase means feeling ill.

practice.prompt: 'Life is a journey.' This is a...
practice.speech: 'Life is a journey.' This is a...
hints: Is there a 'like' or 'as' in the sentence?
With no comparison word, one thing is simply called another.

wrong_feedback.idiom: An idiom is a fixed phrase with a hidden meaning.

practice.explanation: It says life IS a journey, with no 'like' or 'as'.

practice.prompt: 'Break a leg!' said Ma before Uma's dance. What did she mean?
practice.speech: 'Break a leg!' said Ma before Uma's dance. What did she mean?
hints: Would a mother really want her hurt? Think about the situation.
Before a show, this phrase is a good wish.

wrong_feedback.Stop dancing: Ma wants her to dance well.

practice.explanation: It is a wish for success.

practice.prompt: Which sentence is a simile?
practice.speech: Which sentence is a simile?
options: The baby slept like a log
practice.answer: The baby slept like a log
hints: A simile needs the word 'like' or 'as'.
Look for the comparison word in each sentence.

wrong_feedback.The baby was an angel: This says one thing IS another, so it is a metaphor.
wrong_feedback.The baby kicked the ball: This is a plain action, with no comparison.

practice.explanation: 'Like a log' is a comparison with 'like'.

check.prompt: 'He is as stubborn as a mule.' The writer means he is...
check.speech: 'He is as stubborn as a mule.' The writer means he is...

wrong_feedback.very strong: Stubborn is about refusing, not strength.

check.explanation: A mule is known for refusing to move.

check.prompt: 'The moon was a silver coin.' This sentence is a...
check.speech: 'The moon was a silver coin.' This sentence is a...
check.explanation: It says the moon IS a coin, with no comparison word.

check.prompt: 'It's a piece of cake,' said Raj about the maths test. What does he mean?
check.speech: 'It's a piece of cake,' said Raj about the maths test. What does he mean?
options: He ate cake in the test

wrong_feedback.He ate cake in the test: The words are not meant plainly.

check.explanation: The idiom means something very easy.

explain.text: A simile is a comparison with a bridge word, 'like' or 'as'. A metaphor skips the bridge and jumps straight across: A is B.
explain.speech: A simile is a comparison with a bridge word, 'like' or 'as'. A metaphor skips the bridge and jumps straight across: A is B.

explain.text: Read: 'The river was like a silver ribbon' is a simile. 'The river was a silver ribbon' is a metaphor. Same picture, one has a bridge word.
explain.speech: Read: 'The river was like a silver ribbon' is a simile. 'The river was a silver ribbon' is a metaphor. Same picture, one has a bridge word.

explain.text: For an idiom, do not read word by word. Ask what the whole phrase means in that situation.
explain.speech: For an idiom, do not read word by word. Ask what the whole phrase means in that situation.

guided.prompt: 'Her smile was warm as sunshine.' What is this comparison using 'as' called?
guided.speech: 'Her smile was warm as sunshine.' What is this comparison using 'as' called?
guided.answer: a simile
hints: Which figure uses 'as' or 'like'?
Comparison with a bridge word has a special name.

wrong_feedback.an idiom: An idiom is a fixed phrase, not a comparison.

guided.explanation: It compares using 'as'.

guided.prompt: What does 'to burn the midnight oil' mean?
guided.speech: What does 'to burn the midnight oil' mean?
options: To light a lamp for puja
To work late into the night
